L01.materials: Numeral and word cards, place-value mat
L01.induction: Show 400,004 and 440,000. Ask pupils to read both and locate each zero.
L01.model: Model reading 602,015 by grouping the thousands and the remaining digits.
L01.guided_practice: In pairs, match shuffled numerals and number names. Include 1,000,000 and explain one zero placeholder.
L01.assessment: Read 704,016, 890,307 and 610,090 aloud. Write eight hundred thousand and seventeen and nine hundred and forty thousand and five in digits.
L01.evidence: All readings match the numerals. Written answers are 800,017 and 940,005.
L01.closure: Ask pupils to read 500,050 and explain why the final zero is needed.

L02.induction: Underline the 8 in 586,020. Ask where it is and what it is worth.
L02.model: Build 208,061. Record its expansion using a sum of values and using number of units at each place.
L02.guided_practice: Build 390,504 from value cards, exchange an expanded form with a partner and reconstruct the number.
L02.assessment: For 708,305, state the place and value of 8. Expand the number by place and by digit value.
L02.evidence: Thousands and 8,000. Seven hundred thousands + eight thousands + three hundreds + five ones. 700,000 + 8,000 + 300 + 5.
L02.closure: Show 78,005 beside 708,305 and ask how the value of 8 compares.

L03.materials: Place-value chart, numeral cards, number line
L03.induction: Show 654,098 and 645,890. Ask which place first makes them different.
L03.model: Compare from the highest place. Demonstrate how to position an almost equal pair on a number line.
L03.guided_practice: Order five place-value cards and justify both an adjacent pair and the reverse ordering.
L03.assessment: Order 504,680, 540,086, 504,608, 540,068 and 504,860 from smallest to largest. Explain the comparison between 504,608 and 504,680.
L03.evidence: 504,608 < 504,680 < 504,860 < 540,068 < 540,086. The first difference in the selected pair is the tens digit.

L04.materials: Square counters, hundred chart, factor cards
L04.induction: Arrange 9 counters in one row and in a square. Ask what the two arrangements show.
L04.model: Compare 29 with 49 using factors. Explain why 1 has only one distinct factor.
L04.guided_practice: Use arrays or multiplication facts to check 41, 45 and 64. Record factor pairs and agree on a classification.
L04.assessment: Classify 43, 51, 81 and 97. Give a factor pair other than 1 and the number for each composite number.
L04.evidence: 43 and 97 are prime. 51 is 3 × 17 and 81 is 9 × 9, so both are composite.
L04.closure: Ask why 1 is neither prime nor composite.

L05.induction: Compare 328,900 and 329,900. Ask what has changed and by how much.
L05.model: Show an increase of 1,000 crossing a place boundary and a decrease of 10,000 on a number line.
L05.guided_practice: Build an ascending strip from 599,950 with step 10 and a descending strip from 703,500 with step 100.
L05.assessment: Complete 349,750, 350,750, blank, 352,750 and 780,060, blank, 760,060, 750,060. State both rules.
L05.evidence: 351,750 with a step of +1,000. 770,060 with a step of −10,000.
L05.closure: Ask pupils to extend the descending strip by a term and explain the direction.

L06.materials: Identical trays, counters, prepared comparison photo
L06.induction: Show a reference tray of 40 counters. Ask how it can help when the new tray cannot be counted quickly.
L06.model: Compare equal-sized groups at similar density. Show when doubling the reference is a reasonable estimate.
L06.guided_practice: Estimate two prepared trays and count one result to compare with the estimate.
L06.assessment: A tray holds 80 counters. A second same-size tray has about twice the coverage at similar density. Estimate the second count. Its actual count is 152. Explain the estimate difference.
L06.evidence: About 160 counters using 2 × 80. It is 8 above the count, a reasonable difference for an approximate visual comparison.
L06.closure: Ask when unequal density makes this reference misleading.

L07.induction: Show 649,999 and 650,000. Ask whether they round alike to the nearest hundred thousand.
L07.model: Mark the midpoint and explain how to find the first and last whole numbers that round to a stated result.
L07.guided_practice: On two number lines, test boundary points for nearest ten thousand and nearest hundred thousand.
L07.assessment: Round 684,735 to the nearest ten thousand and hundred thousand. Give the full whole-number interval that rounds to 700,000 to the nearest hundred thousand.
L07.evidence: 680,000 and 700,000. The interval is 650,000 to 749,999 inclusive.
L07.closure: Ask pupils to show why 750,000 is outside the interval.

L08.materials: Column-value grid, five number cards, mini-whiteboards
L08.induction: Show 37,450 and 62,580. Ask if their sum should be close to 100,000.
L08.model: Model aligned columns and regrouping when adding several terms. Estimate by rounding each term to the nearest thousand.
L08.guided_practice: Add three terms, check by rearranging the sum and compare exact results with an estimate.
L08.assessment: Add 124,086, 203,714, 7,890, 36,210 and 4,100. Compare the result with an estimate to the nearest thousand for each addend.
L08.closure: Ask what regrouping is needed when ones total more than nine.

L09.induction: Show 500,002 − 1,005. Ask where regrouping needs to start.
L09.model: Record regrouping through zeros and verify the difference by adding back. Extend the method to two deductions.
L09.guided_practice: Calculate two stock balances and circle the columns where a value was exchanged.
L09.assessment: Find 850,024 − 147,605 − 28,919. Show regrouping and verify by restoring both deductions.
L09.closure: Ask pupils to explain why an exchange of one hundred supplies ten tens.

L10.materials: Area grid, multiplication cards, digit chart
L10.induction: Show 37 and ask pupils to split it into useful factors for a partial-products method.
L10.model: Partition 37 into 30 and 7. Align partial products in a grid and estimate the order of magnitude.
L10.guided_practice: Solve a one-digit multiplier, a two-digit multiplier and a multiplication by 100 using place value.
L10.assessment: Find 8,416 × 37, 4,205 × 100 and 386 × 1,000. Explain the partial products in the first calculation.
L10.evidence: 311,392, 420,500 and 386,000. The first calculation uses 252,480 and 58,912.
L10.closure: Ask pupils why the second column of a written multiplication represents tens.

L11.induction: Ask how dividing by 24 is related to grouping by 24 repeatedly.
L11.model: Demonstrate 36,000 ÷ 12. Check each quotient with multiplication and include a place-value check for division by 100.
L11.guided_practice: Solve one long division and one division by a power of ten using different strategies.
L11.assessment: Find 215,136 ÷ 24 and 85,700 ÷ 100. Verify the first answer by multiplication.
L11.closure: Ask pupils to write a multiplication statement for the second answer.

L12.materials: Equation strips, blank cards for unknowns
L12.induction: Reveal only two quantities in 24 × n = 360. Ask which value is missing.
L12.model: Compare finding an unknown factor with finding an unknown dividend. Check by substituting into the original equation.
L12.guided_practice: Sort four equation strips by the position of the unknown. Use inverse operations and check both operation types.
L12.assessment: Find a from 36 × a = 1,404 and b from b ÷ 16 = 325. Check both equations.
L12.evidence: a = 39 and b = 5,200. Both original equations hold after substitution.
L12.closure: Ask when multiplication is used to solve a division equation.

L13.induction: Show 100 + 6 × 8. Ask which part represents six equal groups.
L13.model: Compare 100 + 6 × 8 with (100 + 6) × 8 to explain precedence and brackets.
L13.guided_practice: Mark the first operation in two addition or subtraction expressions involving multiplication.
L13.assessment: Find 32,000 − 480 × 25 and 12 × (160 − 45). Show the first step in both.
L13.evidence: 20,000 and 1,380. Calculate 480 × 25 first in the first expression and 160 − 45 first in the second.

L14.materials: Grouping diagrams, bracket cards, operation strips
L14.induction: Show 80 − 24 ÷ 6. Ask which quantity should be split into groups.
L14.model: Model a subtraction-and-division expression and contrast with division after brackets.
L14.guided_practice: Build expressions from two grouping situations and agree which step to perform first.
L14.assessment: Write and solve an expression for 7,500 more than the result of 36,000 divided by 12. Then evaluate (5,600 − 800) ÷ 24.
L14.evidence: 36,000 ÷ 12 + 7,500 = 10,500. The second expression equals 200, with subtraction first.
L14.closure: Ask pupils to add brackets to show which subtraction occurs before division.

L15.materials: Situation cards, bar models, stock tables
L15.induction: Read a stock problem. Ask which figure is a repeated quantity and which is subtracted once.
L15.model: Model selecting an operation and checking the result against the expected size and unit.
L15.guided_practice: Solve two scenarios with a partner and explain why their operation orders differ.
L15.assessment: Stock starts at 186,500 books. Three deliveries bring 42,750 each and 95,320 are issued. Find the balance. Separately, allocate 4,800 books equally across 24 classes.
L15.evidence: 219,430 books, and 200 per class. Calculations use the correct operations and units.
L15.closure: Ask pupils to name a check for the distribution result.

L16.induction: Show 24 equal cartons with the total hidden. Ask which letter could stand for the total.
L16.model: Connect multiplication and division equations for equal groups. Identify whether the total, group size or group count is unknown.
L16.guided_practice: Build equations for one unknown total and one unknown group size. Check each using the reverse operation.
L16.assessment: Twenty-eight boxes hold 1,624 pens in total. Write an equation and find pens in each box. A stock of badges is shared among 36 groups of 45. Write a division equation and find the stock.
L16.evidence: 28 × n = 1,624 gives 58. b ÷ 36 = 45 gives 1,620. Both equations are checked.
L16.closure: Ask which unknown is the dividend in the badge problem.

R01.induction: Show 504,080 with the value of 8 incorrectly labelled 800. Ask pupils to spot the error.
R01.model: Rebuild the numeral in a place chart. Then model marking brackets or division before evaluating a mixed expression.
R01.guided_practice: Correct a partner's place-value label and show why the first step in their calculation is valid.
R01.assessment: Correct the value of 4 in 640,058 if it is labelled 4,000. Find 86,000 − 18,000 ÷ 6 and check the division.
R01.evidence: The 4 is worth 40,000. The result is 83,000. The division checks as 3,000 × 6 = 18,000.
R01.closure: Ask pupils whether addition or multiplication can check the divided quantity.

L17.materials: Fraction strips, grid paper, fraction cards
L17.induction: Ask how much of a whole half of three quarters should be.
L17.model: Shade 3/4 on a rectangle, then shade 1/2 of that part. Convert a mixed number to an improper fraction before multiplying.
L17.guided_practice: Model two products with grids and explain simplification to a partner.
L17.assessment: Draw 2/3 of 3/4. Also calculate 2 1/4 × 2/3. Give both answers in simplest form.
L17.evidence: Shaded overlap is 1/2. The second product is 1 1/2, using 9/4 × 2/3.
L17.closure: Ask pupils where the denominator comes from in an area model.

L18.induction: Show 6.375. Ask which hundredths are immediately around it.
L18.model: Place 6.375 exactly between 6.37 and 6.38. Compare rounding the same decimal to tenths and hundredths.
L18.guided_practice: On four task cards, mark adjacent allowed values, find midpoints and choose a rounded value.
L18.assessment: Round 7.465 to the nearest whole number, tenth and hundredth. Explain the last result on a number line.
L18.evidence: 7, 7.5 and 7.47. 7.465 is the midpoint between 7.46 and 7.47.
L18.closure: Ask pupils what would change if the starting value were 7.464.

L19.induction: Show 7.2 and 7.20. Ask if they can change position in a written sum.
L19.model: Align the decimal points and append zeros where useful. Model 7.2 − 1.045 + 0.63 from left to right.
L19.guided_practice: Solve two variations and verify one result using a rounded estimate.
L19.assessment: Find 6.8 − 2.037 + 0.54 and 4.275 + 1.6 − 0.89. Record the first result and an estimate for one expression.
L19.evidence: 4.763 then 5.303. 5.875 then 4.985. An estimate close to 5 is reasonable.
L19.closure: Ask which digits should line up when 1.6 and 4.275 are added.

L20.induction: Ask whether 12 × 0.125 is closer to 1 or to 10.
L20.model: Partition 12 into 10 and 2. Then compare the value change when a decimal is multiplied by 100.
L20.guided_practice: Calculate two products with a two-digit multiplier or a power of ten. Explain one digit's change in value.
L20.assessment: Find 0.375 × 16, 0.375 × 100 and 0.375 × 1,000. Show the role of place value in one result.
L20.evidence: 6, 37.5 and 375. Each answer is reasonable against the estimate.
L20.closure: Ask pupils to compare the first factor 0.375 with the result when multiplied by 100.

L21.induction: Ask whether 8.64 ÷ 24 should be above or below 1.
L21.model: Use written division for 4.86 ÷ 12 and check with multiplication. Contrast dividing by 100 and 1,000.
L21.guided_practice: Solve a decimal with a two-digit divisor and two power-of-ten divisions. Identify the place of the leading nonzero digit.
L21.assessment: Find 8.64 ÷ 24, 32.5 ÷ 100 and 325 ÷ 1,000. Verify the first result using multiplication.
L21.closure: Ask why the last two quotients are equal.

L22.materials: Hundred grids, fraction strips, conversion cards
L22.induction: Shade one whole grid and half of a second. Ask how many hundredths are shown.
L22.model: Use a grid and a fraction strip to show 1 3/4 as 175%. Reverse the conversion by separating 100%.
L22.guided_practice: Match a set of mixed numbers and percentages above 100%. Draw one pair to check equivalence.
L22.assessment: Convert 2 1/5 to a percentage and 135% to a mixed number in simplest form. Show the part beyond the first whole.
L22.evidence: 220% and 1 7/20. The parts beyond the first whole are 120 percentage points and 35 percentage points.
L22.closure: Ask which fraction of a whole represents 25%.

L23.induction: Show 100% labelled 80 and ask for the quantity represented by 25%.
L23.model: Build 125% using 100% plus 25%. Model reversing the problem using actual quantity divided by the reference quantity.
L23.guided_practice: Solve one quantity problem and one percentage problem. Label which amount is 100% each time.
L23.assessment: Find 125% of 240 participants. Separately, express 360 as a percentage of 300. Identify both reference amounts.
L23.evidence: 300 participants. 120%. The reference amounts are 240 and 300 respectively.
L23.closure: Ask pupils why the answer in the second question exceeds 100%.

L24.materials: Capacity bar, fraction strips, context cards
L24.induction: Ask how 3/5 and 0.15 can describe parts of the same tank.
L24.model: Label the whole capacity before adding or taking away portions. Model converting the unit of account only after choosing the base.
L24.guided_practice: Use bar models for two situations and identify whether a percentage uses the original or remaining amount.
L24.assessment: A 200 L tank starts 3/5 full. Add 0.15 of full capacity, then remove 10% of full capacity. Separately, find 3/4 of a 32 kg bag of rice.
L24.evidence: 130 L using 120 + 30 − 20. The rice weighs 24 kg. Both answers identify the original whole.
L24.closure: Ask why 10% of the full tank differs from 10% of the current liquid.

R02.induction: Show 1 1/4 and 125%. Ask how pupils could demonstrate equivalence.
R02.model: Review the fraction to percentage link and re-align decimal places in a mixed calculation.
R02.guided_practice: Check a partner's percent conversion and show an inverse check for a decimal result.
R02.assessment: Convert 175% to a mixed number. Find 5.6 − 1.275 + 0.8 and check the subtraction.
R02.closure: Ask pupils to name the place-value mistake that changes 0.8 into 0.08.

L25.materials: Mock invoices, ringgit and sen place grid
L25.induction: Ask pupils to estimate the sum of RM196.75 and RM302.50 before writing a column calculation.
L25.model: Align sen and ringgit on three sample invoices. Show how 160 sen becomes RM1.60.
L25.guided_practice: Combine prices from three display cards, then compare the exact sum with rounded prices.
L25.assessment: Find the sum of RM236,048.75, RM18,502.90 and RM76,450.25. Estimate to the nearest thousand for each amount.
L25.evidence: RM331,001.90. The nearest-thousand estimate is RM331,000, close to the exact total.
L25.closure: Ask how many ringgit can be regrouped from 190 sen.

L26.materials: Budget cards, ringgit and sen grid
L26.induction: Show a budget with two payments. Ask whether both should reduce the starting amount.
L26.model: Show two equivalent ways to find a balance. Verify by adding both payments back to the balance.
L26.guided_practice: Work with a partner to track a balance after each purchase and check one result using addition.
L26.assessment: From RM725,300 deduct RM240,237.15 and RM42,068.80. Verify the balance against the original amount.
L26.evidence: RM442,994.05. Adding both deductions back gives RM725,300.00.
L26.closure: Ask which method makes the intermediate balance visible.

L27.induction: Show RM18.35 per pack. Ask what the unit is after multiplying by the number of packs.
L27.model: Write quantity × unit price. Show place-value changes for groups of 100 and 1,000.
L27.guided_practice: Fill an order table with costs for a two-digit quantity and two powers of ten.
L27.assessment: Calculate the costs of 24 units at RM67.25, 100 units at RM18.35 and 1,000 units at RM2.48. Label each total.
L27.evidence: RM1,614.00, RM1,835.00 and RM2,480.00. Totals are expressed in RM.
L27.closure: Ask how doubling the quantity changes the total cost.

L28.materials: Sharing mats, mock budgets and unit-price cards
L28.induction: Show RM225 split between nine groups. Ask for a reasonable estimate of each share.
L28.model: Demonstrate the connection between dividing by the number of groups and multiplying the share back.
L28.guided_practice: Compare written division with estimating a unit price, including powers-of-ten cases.
L28.assessment: Calculate RM2,437.50 ÷ 25, RM5,650 ÷ 100 and RM7,800 ÷ 1,000. Multiply the first share by 25 to check.
L28.closure: Ask how the answer changes when the same budget is split into more groups.

L29.materials: Price cards, order form, bracket cards
L29.induction: Show a per-set price and a delivery charge. Ask which amount is charged only once.
L29.model: Compare 4 × (RM54.20 + RM12.80) and 4 × RM54.20 + RM12.80. Identify what changes in the order.
L29.guided_practice: Write and compare expressions for a bundle purchase and an extra charge. Rearrange the model without changing the price.
L29.assessment: Three kits each contain items priced RM125.80 and RM94.20. Delivery costs RM45.60 for the whole order. Write one expression and find its value.
L29.evidence: 3 × (RM125.80 + RM94.20) + RM45.60 = RM705.60. Delivery is included once.
L29.closure: Ask what incorrect calculation would charge delivery three times.

L30.induction: Show two statements about saving for a later purchase and investing in a fund. Ask what each aims to do.
L30.model: Explain that investment value can rise or fall. Compare two fictional 5% tables, one based on the original deposit and one on the current balance.
L30.guided_practice: Classify saving and investing examples. Annotate which opening balance each interest method uses in the second year.
L30.assessment: Classify an emergency savings account and a fund bought for possible growth. For a hypothetical RM1,000 deposit at 5% with no withdrawals, compare year-two simple and compound interest.
L30.evidence: Savings and investment respectively. Year two is RM50 on RM1,000 for simple interest, and RM52.50 on RM1,050 for compound interest.
L30.closure: Ask pupils to explain why the compound interest changes even when the rate stays constant.

L31.induction: Show a cash sticker and a monthly payment sticker. Ask which extra information is needed to compare them.
L31.model: Model total instalments plus any deposit. Explain that deferred payment leaves an amount still due.
L31.guided_practice: Compare two fictional offers in a table. Identify the payment at purchase and the amount remaining due immediately after it.
L31.assessment: A tablet costs RM1,050 cash or RM120 down plus 12 payments of RM88.50. Find both totals, the difference and the amount owed after the deposit.
L31.evidence: Cash RM1,050. Credit RM1,182. Difference RM132. RM1,062 remains due under the example terms.
L31.closure: Ask why comparing just one monthly payment and the cash price is misleading.

L32.materials: Club budget sheet, supplier quote cards
L32.induction: Show quantities and unit prices on a quote. Ask which amounts belong in a spending total.
L32.model: Break the spending into unit costs, quantity and a one-time fee. Check the remaining money against a second purchase.
L32.guided_practice: Complete a two-supplier order sheet. Explain what each subtotal includes before comparing it with the budget.
L32.assessment: A club has RM6,000. Buy 18 kits at RM247.50 each and pay RM85 delivery. Can the remainder cover RM1,500 training? Give the shortfall or surplus.
L32.evidence: Spending RM4,540, balance RM1,460, shortage RM40. Delivery is included once.
L32.closure: Ask pupils to justify whether the training cost is part of the first purchase total.

R03.materials: Cash and credit offer cards, balance table
R03.induction: Show a one-time cash amount and eight equal instalments. Ask which values must be combined.
R03.model: Revisit the difference between an amount owed and a total price. Model checking a budget balance by addition.
R03.guided_practice: Make and check a comparison table for two offers. Explain which cost is counted once.
R03.assessment: A bike costs RM540 cash or nine instalments of RM64. Find the credit total and difference. If a family pays cash from RM800, find the balance and check it.
R03.evidence: Credit RM576, difference RM36. Cash balance RM260, checked by RM540 + RM260 = RM800.
R03.closure: Ask what other charge would have to be included if the credit offer added a deposit.

L33.induction: Ask how much time passes from 23:00 to 01:00 the next day.
L33.model: Break an interval at midnight for days and hours. For longer calendar intervals, count elapsed days across months and include 29 February in a leap year.
L33.guided_practice: Find a days-and-hours interval on a timeline. Count the days from 26 February to 2 March in a leap year and in a common year.
L33.assessment: Use days and hours from Tuesday 09:00 to Thursday 15:00. Find the elapsed days from 12 April to 19 June and from 14 February 2024 to 20 May 2026.
L33.evidence: 2 days 6 hours. 68 days. 826 days, including 29 February 2024. Count elapsed dates at the same time of day.
L33.closure: Ask why crossing midnight once does not always mean 24 hours have elapsed.

L34.materials: Fraction strips, clock diagram, conversion chart
L34.induction: Ask how many hours equal half of a day.
L34.model: Use the whole unit before multiplying by a fraction. Show how conversion back restores the starting quantity.
L34.guided_practice: Match fractional time cards and check pairs by reversing the conversion.
L34.assessment: Convert 2 1/4 hours to minutes, 5/6 day to hours and 1 3/4 years to months. Show an inverse check for two conversions.
L34.evidence: 135 minutes, 20 hours and 21 months. Examples of checks are 135 ÷ 60 = 2 1/4 and 20 ÷ 24 = 5/6.
L34.closure: Ask how changing the whole unit changes the multiplier.

L35.materials: Clock diagram, decimal cards, time conversion chart
L35.induction: Ask whether 1.5 hours and 1 hour 50 minutes are equal.
L35.model: Split 1.35 hours into one hour and 0.35 hour. Multiply the fractional part by 60 and compare with daily units.
L35.guided_practice: Convert decimal quantities in a matching activity. Use smaller units and explain the role of 60 or 24.
L35.assessment: Convert 1.75 days to hours, 0.35 hour to minutes and 2.4 decades to years. Explain why 0.35 hour is not 35 minutes.
L35.evidence: 42 hours, 21 minutes and 24 years. A decimal part of an hour is multiplied by 60.
L35.closure: Ask pupils to convert 0.2 hour without using a clock.

L36.materials: Timeline strips, fraction cards, decimal duration chart
L36.induction: Show 1/2 hour and 0.5 hour. Ask what both represent on the same clock.
L36.model: Convert fractional hours and decimal days to a chosen common unit. Add examples before re-expressing in larger units.
L36.guided_practice: Work out one sum in minutes and one sum in hours. Check using the original units on a bar model.
L36.assessment: Find 1 1/2 hours + 3/4 hour in minutes and 2.75 days + 0.5 day in hours. Show the conversions.
L36.closure: Ask pupils to explain why hours and days cannot be combined as bare numbers.

L37.materials: Number lines, clock model, elapsed-time cards
L37.induction: Show 3.4 hours. Ask how to represent the 0.4 hour in minutes before subtracting.
L37.model: Work through a fractional duration and a decimal duration. Demonstrate checking the difference by addition.
L37.guided_practice: Compare two subtraction paths and write an inverse check for the result from a partner's card.
L37.assessment: Find 2 3/4 hours − 5/6 hour in minutes and 3.4 hours − 1.15 hours in hours and minutes. Verify one.
L37.evidence: 115 minutes and 2 hours 15 minutes. An inverse check is 115 + 50 = 165 minutes.
L37.closure: Ask when converting to minutes avoids fractional borrowing.

L38.induction: Show departure at 08:35 and arrival after a stop. Ask which events go on the timeline.
L38.model: Model adding travel segments and a break, then subtracting backward from a finishing time.
L38.guided_practice: Draw journeys from two cards and distinguish travel time from total elapsed time.
L38.assessment: A bus leaves at 08:35, drives 1 hour 45 minutes, stops 25 minutes and drives 50 minutes. Find arrival time. For an event ending at 15:20 after 45, 20 and 55 minutes, find the start.
L38.evidence: Bus arrives at 11:35. Event starts at 13:20. Include the stop and the break in the respective elapsed times.
L38.closure: Ask which duration should be omitted if only driving time is requested.

R04.materials: Calendar and clock strips, correction cards
R04.induction: Show 2.25 hours labelled 2 hours 25 minutes. Ask pupils to check it.
R04.model: Compare a real clock calculation with a decimal conversion. Use a timed itinerary as a second example.
R04.guided_practice: Explain one corrected conversion to a partner and mark the turnaround on a daily schedule.
R04.assessment: Find elapsed time from 09:45 to 12:10. Correct the claim that 2.25 hours is 2 hours 25 minutes.
R04.evidence: 2 hours 25 minutes elapsed. 2.25 hours is 2 hours 15 minutes.
R04.closure: Ask how a decimal fraction of an hour differs from a time shown on a clock.

L39.materials: Ruler, tape measure, metric conversion table
L39.induction: Show 1 m and 1 cm. Ask how many units of one fit in the other.
L39.model: Use a conversion chain from millimetres to kilometres. Compare decimal and fraction forms for the same length.
L39.guided_practice: Measure two strips and record equivalent values in two units. Convert a route distance back to the original unit.
L39.assessment: Convert 7 1/2 mm to cm as a fraction, 472.5 cm to metres and 1.275 km to metres. Reverse one conversion.
L39.evidence: 3/4 cm, 4.725 m and 1,275 m. The inverse calculation restores the original measure.
L39.closure: Ask when converting a length to a larger unit makes the number smaller.

L40.materials: Tape measure, ribbon segments, metric table
L40.induction: Show 0.75 m and 65 cm. Ask whether the numerals alone reveal the longer ribbon.
L40.model: Convert to a common unit before adding or subtracting. Show where to record the unit in every step.
L40.guided_practice: Build lengths from three ribbon cards. Record total and leftover length in a unit selected by a partner.
L40.assessment: Find the sum of 0.85 m, 125 cm and 1 3/4 m. Separately subtract 125 cm and 3/4 m from 4.6 m. Give both results in metres.
L40.evidence: 3.85 m and 2.6 m. All three quantities are in metres before operating.
L40.closure: Ask why 125 cannot be added to 0.85 without a conversion.

L41.induction: Show a ribbon cut into equal pieces. Ask when to multiply and when to divide.
L41.model: Work through repeated lengths in centimetres and equal sections measured in metres. Estimate the length of one section before division.
L41.guided_practice: Find the total of several equal spans and reverse the calculation for one span. Use metric units at each step.
L41.assessment: Find the total of 16 strips of 0.375 m in cm. Split 3 3/4 m into 15 equal pieces and give one piece in cm.
L41.evidence: 600 cm and 25 cm. A check for the second is 25 cm × 15 = 375 cm.
L41.closure: Ask whether dividing a total gives an answer larger or smaller than the starting measure.

L42.induction: Show 625 g on a scale. Ask how to describe it in kilograms in two forms.
L42.model: Use 1,000 g = 1 kg to explain 625 g = 0.625 kg = 5/8 kg.
L42.guided_practice: Match package labels written in grams, fractional kilograms and decimal kilograms. Reverse a conversion to check.
L42.assessment: Convert 2 3/4 kg to grams, 1,125 g to kilograms as a mixed number and 350 g to kilograms as a decimal.
L42.evidence: 2,750 g, 1 1/8 kg and 0.35 kg. Each answer names the requested unit.
L42.closure: Ask pupils what mass 1/4 kg represents in grams.

L43.materials: Mass cards, scales or sample packages, conversion table
L43.induction: Show 3.2 kg and 350 g. Ask whether these can be combined before converting.
L43.model: Use grams or kilograms consistently. Demonstrate how to include three terms and verify a difference by addition.
L43.guided_practice: Use a table of three package masses to find a sum and then the mass remaining after two are removed.
L43.assessment: Add 1.625 kg, 850 g and 2 1/4 kg. Then subtract 850 g and 1 1/4 kg from 6.35 kg. Give both in kilograms.
L43.evidence: 4.725 kg and 4.25 kg. 850 g is 0.85 kg in both calculations.
L43.closure: Ask how to check a mass balance without doing the subtraction again.

L44.materials: Recipe strips, weighing scale, equal-share cards
L44.induction: Show a 0.375 kg bag. Ask how two bags compare with a kilogram.
L44.model: Scale a quantity for repeated portions. For division, convert to grams before equally sharing when helpful.
L44.guided_practice: Calculate a batch mass and a single portion mass. Explain where the conversion fits in each calculation.
L44.assessment: Find the mass of 16 bags of 0.375 kg. Divide 15 3/4 kg into 25 equal packets and give one packet in grams.
L44.evidence: 6 kg and 630 g per packet. 630 g × 25 = 15,750 g.
L44.closure: Ask when changing to grams makes an equal-share calculation easier.

L45.materials: Graduated jugs, litre strip, conversion cards
L45.induction: Show a jug marked at 250 mL and ask what fraction of a litre it holds.
L45.model: Use graduations to connect 1/4 L with 250 mL. Demonstrate fractional and decimal forms with two further marks.
L45.guided_practice: Match litre labels to millilitre graduations, then verify a fraction form by multiplying back.
L45.assessment: Convert 2 3/8 L to mL, 1,650 mL to L as a decimal and 375 mL to L as a simplified fraction. Check one.
L45.closure: Ask how many millilitres make up 0.125 L.

L46.materials: Measuring jug, tank model, metric place chart
L46.induction: Show 850 mL and 0.85 L. Ask whether the values are equal.
L46.model: Record volumes in one unit before combining containers. Check a remaining volume by adding the removed quantities back.
L46.guided_practice: Make total and remaining-volume examples from three measurements and compare two unit choices.
L46.assessment: Add 1 3/4 L, 825 mL and 0.95 L. Then remove 850 mL and 1 3/4 L from 4.25 L. Give both answers in litres.
L46.evidence: 3.525 L and 1.65 L. The subtraction is 4.25 − 0.85 − 1.75.
L46.closure: Ask which writing makes it easier to keep three decimal places aligned.

L47.materials: Container labels, measuring jug, sharing table
L47.induction: Show a bottle with 0.275 L. Ask how to calculate the amount in several identical bottles.
L47.model: Contrast repeated volume with equal sharing. Show a reverse multiplication check after unit conversion.
L47.guided_practice: Fill a table of container counts, total volumes and individual capacities. Use both litres and millilitres.
L47.assessment: Find the volume of 36 bottles of 0.275 L in mL. Split 3.6 L equally among 24 bottles and give the volume of one in mL.
L47.evidence: 9,900 mL in total and 150 mL per bottle. 24 × 150 mL = 3.6 L.
L47.closure: Ask what changes if the number of bottles doubles while the total stays fixed.

L48.materials: Measurement problem cards, metric conversion chart
L48.induction: Show a 45 cm cut on an 8.5 m roll. Ask what needs to share a unit.
L48.model: Model three steps: identify units, calculate the repeated quantity, and compare with the available amount.
L48.guided_practice: Solve one stock problem with length and one with mass. Explain whether each answer describes a total, a remainder or a shortfall.
L48.assessment: Cut twelve 45 cm pieces from an 8.5 m rope. Can the remainder yield seven more? Separately, from 8.25 kg of flour use twelve portions of 475 g. Find the remaining mass.
L48.evidence: Rope remainder 3.1 m, 0.05 m short of 3.15 m. Flour remainder 2.55 kg.
L48.closure: Ask why comparing both requirements with stock uses the same structure despite different units.

R05.materials: Mixed measure cards, rulers, scales, measuring jugs
R05.induction: Show 0.75 m, 0.75 kg and 0.75 L. Ask which instrument or unit belongs to each.
R05.model: Review two ways to convert a measurement. Check a combined measurement by solving in both compatible units.
R05.guided_practice: Select measuring tools and justify the chosen units. Trade two calculations for an inverse check.
R05.assessment: Find 1 1/4 m + 85 cm in cm. Find 2.5 kg − 750 g in kg. Verify one answer with the reverse operation.
R05.evidence: 210 cm and 1.75 kg. A valid check is 1.75 kg + 0.75 kg = 2.5 kg.
R05.closure: Ask why metre, kilogram and litre measurements cannot be added together.

L49.materials: Regular and irregular polygon cards, ruler, folding paper
L49.induction: Show a square and a non-square rectangle. Ask whether both have equal sides and equal angles.
L49.model: Compare equal sides and interior angles. Use a square to distinguish its sides, vertices, lines of symmetry, interior angles and diagonals.
L49.guided_practice: Classify an equilateral triangle and a regular hexagon, then mark a line of symmetry and a diagonal where possible.
L49.assessment: Classify a square and a rhombus with 60° and 120° angles. For the square, record the number of sides, vertices, axes, interior angles and diagonals.
L49.evidence: The square is regular and the rhombus has unequal angles. Square: four sides, four vertices, four axes, four 90° interior angles and two diagonals.
L49.closure: Ask which property a square has in addition to equal sides.

L50.materials: Protractors, rulers, full-size regular polygon outlines
L50.induction: Show a polygon vertex. Ask where the centre of a protractor should be placed.
L50.model: Model lining up a side with zero and reading the scale that starts there. Demonstrate with a triangle and a pentagon.
L50.guided_practice: Measure three angles on two prepared outlines. Exchange measurements and recheck discrepant readings.
L50.assessment: Measure two interior angles each in a regular pentagon and a regular hexagon. Identify the larger kind.
L50.evidence: Pentagon 108°, hexagon 120°, within 2°. Hexagon angles are larger by about 12°.
L50.closure: Ask pupils to identify the error when a pentagon interior angle is read as 72°.

L51.materials: Square and equilateral triangle cutouts, rulers, grid paper
L51.induction: Join two shapes along one same-length edge. Ask which sides are still visible from outside.
L51.model: Trace the outer path and compare it with the sum of the two original perimeters. Remove two copies of the shared length.
L51.guided_practice: Construct two composites, label each exposed edge and check the answer by subtraction.
L51.assessment: A square of side 6 cm shares one side with an equilateral triangle of side 6 cm. Sketch the shape and find its perimeter.
L51.evidence: Five outside edges measure 6 cm each. The perimeter is 30 cm.
L51.closure: Ask why the shared edge is removed twice when starting from both perimeters.

L52.induction: Show an L-shaped grid. Ask where a straight cut creates two rectangles.
L52.model: Demonstrate partitioning an L-shape into two rectangles and finding the same area by subtracting a corner from the enclosing rectangle.
L52.guided_practice: Find a composite area in two ways. Check that the rectangles cover the figure with neither overlap nor gaps.
L52.assessment: Draw a 9 cm by 6 cm rectangle with a 3 cm by 2 cm corner cut away. Find the remaining area and label both parts of one valid partition.
L52.evidence: 48 cm². For example, use 9 × 4 and 6 × 2, or 54 − 6.
L52.closure: Ask why square centimetres are the correct unit even when side lengths are in centimetres.

L53.materials: Unit cubes, cube and cuboid diagrams
L53.induction: Join a cube to a cuboid without overlap. Ask how the total volume can be found.
L53.model: Use unit cubes to show length × width × height. Add the two separate volumes and explain the cubic unit.
L53.guided_practice: Build a small composite solid, measure each part and compare a calculation with a cube count.
L53.assessment: A cube of side 3 cm is attached to a cuboid measuring 3 cm by 5 cm by 2 cm without overlap. Find the total volume.
L53.evidence: 27 cm³ + 30 cm³ = 57 cm³. Each component is counted once.
L53.closure: Ask how an overlap would change the partition and the total.

L54.materials: Scale-free floor and container diagrams, unit cards
L54.induction: Show a floor, a fence and a stack of boxes. Ask what each question would measure.
L54.model: Choose perimeter, area or volume from each question and link the choice to the unit used in the result.
L54.guided_practice: Sort context cards by measure. Solve one with a partner and explain which lengths are needed.
L54.assessment: Find the exposed edge for a 12 m by 8 m garden with a 4 m square attached along one 4 m edge. Find the area to tile on a 6 m by 5 m floor after excluding a 2 m by 2 m section.
L54.evidence: Fence 48 m, as 40 + 16 − 8. Tiling area 26 m², as 30 − 4. Units match the questions.
L54.closure: Ask how the method would change if the question involved capacity of joined solid parts.

R06.induction: Show a floor plan and an edge trace in two colours. Ask which feature each colour describes.
R06.model: Review choosing a measure first, then checking its unit. Demonstrate one partition for a cut-away rectangle.
R06.guided_practice: Make a question about the shape for a partner and label whether its answer is a length, area or volume.
R06.assessment: From a 7 cm by 5 cm rectangle remove a 2 cm by 2 cm corner. Choose the measure for covering the remainder and calculate it. Explain why the unit fits.
R06.evidence: Area 31 cm². The cover uses squares of side 1 cm, so the result is in square centimetres.
R06.closure: Ask how a question about fencing the outline changes the chosen measure.

L55.induction: Plot (2, 3) and ask which coordinate controls each direction.
L55.model: Show horizontal and vertical segments from the origin, then between two points. Count intervals between grid lines.
L55.guided_practice: Plot one set of two points and label each segment with its distance in grid units.
L55.assessment: Find horizontal and vertical distances from O(0, 0) to A(2, 3), and from A to B(9, 7). Draw and label the two directions.
L55.evidence: O–A is 2 units horizontally and 3 vertically. A–B is 7 horizontally and 4 vertically.
L55.closure: Ask why two points on one row have zero vertical distance.

L56.materials: Counters in two colours, grouping mats
L56.induction: Show 9 red and 15 blue counters. Ask what changes when the requested order is reversed.
L56.model: Represent part to part, part to whole and whole to part. Circle the words that set the order.
L56.guided_practice: Build two-colour groups and write three ordered ratios for each. Read them to a partner.
L56.assessment: A tray has 9 red and 15 blue counters. Write and interpret red to blue, blue to all and all to red.
L56.evidence: 9 : 15, 15 : 24 and 24 : 9, or equivalent ratios in the specified order. There are 24 counters in all.
L56.closure: Ask pupils to identify which ratio becomes its reverse when the wording is reversed.

L57.induction: Show six identical notebooks costing RM27. Ask what one notebook costs.
L57.model: Find the unit value and use it to scale up or down at a constant price. Show a check using an equivalent ratio.
L57.guided_practice: Complete a table for multiple quantities, then find a missing quantity from a stated cost.
L57.assessment: At the same fixed rate, six notebooks cost RM27. Find the cost of ten and the number that cost RM54. Show the unit price.
L57.evidence: RM4.50 per notebook, RM45 for ten and twelve notebooks for RM54.
L57.closure: Ask when a quantity discount would invalidate use of the same unit price.

L58.materials: First-quadrant school map, ratio strip, unit-rate tables
L58.induction: Show a route that turns once. Ask how to describe each part using the grid.
L58.model: Find the horizontal and vertical distances between two landmarks. Separately model using one unit value in a pricing problem.
L58.guided_practice: Work on a map task and a proportional shopping task. Label the units in both solutions.
L58.assessment: On a grid, move from (2, 1) to (8, 5) horizontally then vertically. State both grid distances and the total. At a fixed price, four drink packs cost RM18. Find the cost of ten.
L58.evidence: 6 units and 4 units, total 10 grid units. The packs cost RM45 using RM4.50 per pack.
L58.closure: Ask why a path with a right-angle turn differs from a straight diagonal.

R07.materials: Labelled grids, two-colour counters and price cards
R07.induction: Show two coordinates with equal y values. Ask which distance remains zero.
R07.model: Check a grid distance using differences in coordinates. Revisit why the order of two quantities matters in a ratio.
R07.guided_practice: Trade a grid check and a ratio interpretation with a partner.
R07.assessment: Check the horizontal and vertical distances from (4, 2) to (4, 9). A box has 8 green and 12 yellow counters. Give yellow to all and explain its terms.
R07.evidence: 0 horizontally and 7 units vertically. Yellow to all is 12 : 20 or 3 : 5. Both relate the yellow count to the total.
R07.closure: Ask how the requested ratio would change for all to yellow.

L59.materials: Teacher-made labelled pie charts, hundred grid
L59.induction: Show 60% and 25% sectors. Ask which represents more observations.
L59.model: Link sector labels to counts when the total is known. Show why the percentages in a full pie add to 100%.
L59.guided_practice: Use a pie chart to find one missing share and compare the counts of two sectors.
L59.assessment: In a pie chart of 80 pupils, badminton is 40%, football 35%, netball 15% and table tennis 10%. Find netball's count and the difference between the two largest categories.
L59.evidence: 12 for netball. Badminton has 32 and football 28, so their difference is 4 pupils.
L59.closure: Ask why comparing percentages from two surveys requires checking their totals to compare counts.

L60.materials: Sortable data cards, tally grid, small whiteboards
L60.induction: Show an unsorted dataset. Ask which value appears most and what needs to happen before finding the median.
L60.model: Order the values. Demonstrate frequency for mode, midpoint for median, sum divided by count for mean, and max minus min for range.
L60.guided_practice: Calculate four measures for datasets of odd and even sizes. Exchange the ordered lists to check the calculations.
L60.assessment: For 8, 12, 6, 15, 8 and 11, give the ordered list, mode, median, mean and range. Show the median and mean calculations.
L60.closure: Ask what happens to the mean when one value becomes much larger.

L61.materials: Two team tables, labelled pie chart
L61.induction: Ask how two groups can have the same mean but different ranges.
L61.model: Calculate one measure for a group's typical result and another for spread. Demonstrate comparing two sectors in a pie chart.
L61.guided_practice: Pick a meaningful measure for a claim about consistency. Explain which sector comparison answers a second question.
L61.assessment: Compare consistency of sets A: 4, 6, 8, 10 and B: 6, 7, 7, 8. In a pie chart of 60 pupils, compare the counts for 30% and 20%.
L61.evidence: Both means are 7. Ranges 6 and 2 show B is more consistent by range. Chart counts are 18 and 12, a difference of 6.
L61.closure: Ask which measure directly shows how far apart the minimum and maximum are.

R08.materials: Pie chart of reading choices, ordered data cards
R08.induction: Show a whole pie split into halves and quarters. Ask how the angles relate to the shares.
R08.model: Review finding a count from a sector and choosing a measure that answers a precise question.
R08.guided_practice: Explain one count from the chart to a partner. Check the measure used to answer a question about frequent results.
R08.assessment: A pie chart of 40 pupils has sectors of 50%, 25%, 15% and 10%. Find the two largest counts. For books read 2, 3, 3, 4, 8, select the measure that tells the most frequent value.
R08.evidence: Largest counts 20 and 10. Mode gives the most frequent value, which is 3 books.
R08.closure: Ask which measure instead gives the middle number of books read.
